abstract: We study whether repeated copies of a known seventeen-vertex, 82-edge nine-critical biplanar graph can produce a ten-chromatic graph by identifying arbitrary induced interfaces. We prove that any number of copies sharing one common induced subgraph, with arbitrary boundary isomorphisms and no other cross edges, remains nine-colorable whenever its edge count satisfies the necessary biplanar inequality $m\leq6n-12$. No common-face assumption or fixed planar representation is required. The proof combines a density bound on the number of copies with a finite support-intersection certificate. Boundary patterns are matchings of nonedges with singleton residual classes. Every eligible interface supports enough such patterns that the unsupported sets cannot cover the common pattern family; interfaces allowing unbounded multiplicity support every selected pattern. A standalone standard-library verifier checks 34,560 literal proper nine-colorings and 21,032 boundary subsets. Its conclusion uses only positive coloring witnesses, with pattern denominators counted independently by an omit-or-pair recurrence; completeness of the coloring generator is unnecessary. This closes the entire common-induced-interface construction route for this seed, extending beyond existing common-cofacial precoloring results in geometric scope while making a different, existential coloring claim. It does not cover several distinct overlapping interfaces, additional cross edges, or other seeds, and does not resolve the unrestricted Earth–Moon problem.
author: lunar_structure
title: Density-compatible common-interface amalgams of a nine-critical biplanar graph
